description: Hello! We are a team of 3 engineers of Tucuman, thriving to live this challenge of data manipulation and analysis
summary: PyroForesee is an interactive geospatial web application fire database that unifies active fire detections from NASA's MODIS ('Terra', 'Aqua') and VIIRS ('S-NPP', 'NOAA-20', 'NOAA-21') into a single comparable monthly series ranging from 2012-01 to 2026-08.
details:
Because newer VIIRS sensors spot smaller fires than older MODIS sensors, simply adding satellite counts together makes recent years look like they have far more fires even when fire activity did not change. To fix this, PyroForesee starts from 588,784,736 official archive fire records, keeps only vegetation fires with medium or high confidence (greater than 30%), and summarizes them into 0.25-degree global grid cells (about 28 km per side at the equator, 1,036,800 cells worldwide).

Instead of summing multiple afternoon satellites that fly over the same fire less than an hour apart, each month uses a single reference satellite (S-NPP from 2012 to 2019, NOAA-20 from 2020 to 2026, NOAA-21 as a backup in July 2023, and Aqua directly in August 2026). That sensor's counts and Fire Radiative Power (heat energy in Megawatts) are scaled using 648 regional and seasonal calibration factors so everything reads what MODIS Aqua would have detected during its stable 2012-2020 orbit.

On the website, users move or zoom the map anywhere in the world to pick an Area of Interest (AOI) and see three main tools:

1. Burning Activity Calendar (2012-2026): A year-by-month heatmap comparing every month against the same calendar month in all other valid years. It highlights quiet months, moderate increases (50-75%, 75-90%), extreme months (above 90%), all-time highs, and robust logarithmic z-scores, while clearly hatching months that had satellite outages or partial coverage instead of hiding them or showing them as zero.

2. Interactive Map and Sensor Breakdown: Shows harmonized gridded fire totals and heat density (MW per square kilometer) across the selected region, automatically switching to 1-degree blocks when zoomed far out to stay fast. Users can also inspect individual satellite counts (keeping morning-orbit Terra separate) or switch to sensor footprint views (375 m VIIRS vs. 1 km MODIS).

What benefits does it have?

- Removes false jumps and double counting: Prevents artificial spikes when NOAA-20 (2018) and NOAA-21 (2023) launched and avoids counting the same wildfire up to three times in one afternoon.

- Proven accuracy: Testing by leaving one full year out at a time shows error drops from 43.1% on a single 0.25-degree cell to 27.9% on a 1-degree block and 8.2% at regional latitude-band scale, with near-zero bias (-1.2% to +2.0%).

What is the intended impact?

PyroForesee helps firefighters, land managers, environmental agencies (such as CONAE and regional forestry services), and scientists tell real climate and land-use fire emergencies apart from changes in satellite hardware or shifting satellite pass times.

What tools, coding languages, software, or hardware did we use?

- Database and Data Pipeline: PostgreSQL 18, SQL, Python 3.13.

- Backend Web API: FastAPI.

- Frontend Web App: React 18, TypeScript, Vite.

- Containers and Deployment: Docker, Docker Compose, Git.

How is our project creative?

- Fast map queries without heavy GIS plugins: Any map window (even across the +/-180-degree date line) is converted into consecutive numeric cell ID ranges in PostgreSQL, keeping 15-year regional summaries fast without PostGIS overhead.

- Honest empty-month handling: Because quiet cells are omitted from the main table to save space, a dedicated 176-month reference table keeps data-quality flags intact even when a small area had zero fires that month.

What factors did our team consider?

- Satellite orbit drift: Terra's morning pass shifted earlier to around 9:27 AM by 2026 and Aqua's afternoon pass shifted to around 3:27 PM, so Terra stays separate and August 2026 (Aqua-only) displays an explicit ~10% underestimation notice.

- Short-window bias and extreme fires: We used monthly totals (as recommended by NASA's MODIS guide to avoid 8-day cloud/orbit gaps) and percentiles plus median-based z-scores so a few massive wildfires do not distort normal averages.

- Scale limits and visual accessibility: Because a single 0.25-degree cell has higher uncertainty (43.1%) and polar/extreme latitude bands (-60 deg, 70 deg) have fewer training fires, the interface automatically warns users when an area has fewer than 4 cells or crosses low-confidence latitude bands. The calendar uses colorblind-safe colors, cross-hatched quality alerts, and supports both English and Spanish.
